strengths: The core empirical finding — that self-supervised speech representations (HuBERT/wav2vec2/WavLM) can be linearly mapped to EMG muscle power (r = 0.85) and that EMG power vectors cluster by articulatory gesture — is an interesting and plausibly useful characterization of what SS speech models encode, with a nice mechanistic interpretation of why HuBERT layer 6 works well for resynthesis.

The planned open-source corpus (9 hours, ~6,800 words, natural speaking rate ~115 wpm, alignment-free setting) addresses a genuine gap in EMG-to-speech research, where prior work relies on small-vocabulary or privately held data.

The covariance/SPD representation of EMG with a Cholesky-based geodesic distance is a reasonable and somewhat novel featurization, and the k-medoids gesture-clustering experiment (73.7% vs 10% chance) gives quantitative support to the claim that these features encode articulatory structure.
The data collection protocol, electrode placement, preprocessing, and ethical statement are described in reasonable detail.
The alignment-free CTC-based training setup (EMG -> discrete HuBERT units -> vocoder) follows a sensible, established pipeline.
weaknesses: The headline claim — end-to-end EMG-to-audio synthesis — is never actually evaluated. There is no listening test, no intelligibility metric (WER/CER are explicitly deferred to 'continuing work'), and no audio examples. The synthesis claim in the title and abstract is therefore unsupported.

The reported decoding results are weak and lack context: UER of 58.7% and PER of 41.4% are extremely high, and there is no baseline comparison whatsoever (e.g., against Gaddy & Klein [7, 8] or any prior EMG-to-speech system), so it is impossible to judge whether this represents progress.

Reproducibility claims are contradictory: the paper repeatedly criticizes prior work for private datasets and non-reproducible pipelines and claims to 'open-source' the corpus, but footnote 2 states data and code 'will be made publicly available upon completion of the project.' Nothing is currently available. The IRB protocol field is left blank and the conflict-of-interest section is empty, suggesting the manuscript is incomplete.

There appears to be conceptual confusion about the pipeline: the abstract claims synthesis 'without ... vocoder training,' yet a pretrained Tacotron is used as the 'vocoder'; Tacotron is a TTS model, not a vocoder (the HuBERT-unit resynthesis literature uses HiFi-GAN unit vocoders), so the audio-generation component is underspecified.

The linear-probe analysis may overstate novelty and strength: correlation between SS features and EMG power is expected since both correlate with speech energy/articulator movement; the authors' own control (audio spectrogram vs D(E), r = 0.61) shows a substantial baseline that is not fully analyzed. The claim of providing a 'principled interpretation' for the layer-6 peak is speculative — the analysis shows correlation, not mechanism.

Evaluation details are thin: number of subjects for the main decoding experiments, speaker-dependent vs speaker-independent splits, and what the ±std in Tables 1–2 is computed over are not stated. The gesture dataset (12 subjects, 22 electrodes) is a separate, smaller collection from the main corpus, which weakens the transfer of the 5.1/5.2 findings to the synthesis system.

The paper reads as work-in-progress: Section 6 ('Continuing work') describes core evaluations (phoneme-guided decoding, WER/CER, perceptual assessment) as future work, confirming that the central contributions are not yet complete.

strengths: The paper introduces a large-vocabulary EMG-speech corpus (~9 hours, ~6,800 unique words at natural speaking rate), which addresses a genuine resource gap in the silent-speech/EMG literature where prior work relied on small or private datasets.

The analysis section (Sections 5.1-5.2) is reasonably well motivated: probing the linear relationship between self-supervised speech representations and EMG power, and showing gesture-level cluster structure, provides a somewhat novel interpretability angle that connects to prior EMA probing work (Cho et al.) and offers a plausible explanation for why intermediate HuBERT layers work well for resynthesis.
The alignment-free problem setting (unknown EMG-to-audio alignment, CTC-based training) is more challenging and more practically relevant than prior EMG-to-speech work that assumed known alignments.
The data collection methodology is described in operational detail (electrode placement, amplifier, filtering, synchronization), and an ethical statement is included.
weaknesses: The central claim - synthesizing intelligible speech from EMG - is not actually evaluated. There is no perceptual listening test, no objective audio-quality metric (PESQ, MCD, WER of synthesized audio), and no demonstration that the decoded HuBERT units, at 58.7% UER, produce comprehensible speech at all. The authors themselves acknowledge in Section 6 that methods to 'objectively assess the perceptual quality of the synthesized audio' are future work. A paper titled 'emg2speech' whose synthesis quality is entirely unmeasured cannot support its headline contribution.

No external baselines or comparisons. The evaluation is restricted to an internal comparison of three EMG feature representations (vec(E), D(E), vec(B)) on one architecture. There is no comparison against prior EMG-to-speech systems (e.g., Gaddy & Klein) or even simpler alternatives, so neither the dataset difficulty nor the method's competitiveness can be judged.

Reproducibility commitments are unmet: data and code are only promised 'upon completion of the project.' For a paper whose stated motivation includes addressing 'private datasets, lack of reproducible benchmarks, and opaque architectures,' releasing nothing is a significant credibility problem. Training details (hyperparameters, optimization, number of subjects in the main corpus, speaker-dependent vs. speaker-independent splits) are also missing.

The causal/explanatory claims outrun the evidence. The interpretation that layer-6 HuBERT is optimal for resynthesis *because* it encodes articulatory power is a correlation-based conjecture; the correlation of r=0.85 could partly reflect shared energy/loudness structure rather than articulatory content, and no controls, significance tests, or alternative explanations are analyzed.

Internal inconsistencies and unfinished writing reduce clarity: D(E) is described as 31-dimensional in Section 5.3 but gestures use 22 electrodes; the main corpus participant count is never stated; the IRB statement contains an incomplete sentence; the Conflict of Interest section is empty; and key design choices (e.g., why 22 of 31 electrodes for the gesture study) are relegated to footnotes.

The probing in Section 5.2 is performed on a proxy (D(E)) rather than the full covariance, admitted in a lengthy footnote, and the gesture dataset is a separately collected, single-frame dataset from only 12 subjects at 70-74% clustering accuracy over 13 classes - modest evidence on which to build the paper's central theoretical narrative.

As it stands, the best reported result (41.42% phoneme error rate) is far from a usable communication interface, and without audio evaluation there is no evidence the pipeline yields functional speech; the paper reads as an interim project report rather than a complete study.

strengths: The paper collects and (eventually) releases a large-vocabulary EMG-speech corpus (~9 hours, ~6,800 words, natural speaking rate ~115 wpm), addressing a real scarcity of alignment-free, natural-rate EMG speech data; most prior EMG-to-speech work uses private, small-vocabulary corpora with known alignments.

The analysis pipeline is clearly motivated and generally well executed: the SPD covariance representation D(E), the Cholesky-based geodesic metric, and the gesture-clustering experiment (70.6%/73.7% vs. 10% chance) provide a coherent story that EMG power encodes articulatory structure.

The linear probing of self-supervised speech representations against D(E) (r = 0.85) is a clean, interpretable analysis, and the observation that the HuBERT layer-6 peak aligns with the layer known to be optimal for resynthesis gives a plausible mechanistic interpretation of prior empirical findings.

The comparison across feature pairs (H-D(E) r=0.85 vs. H-B r=0.57, A-D(E) r=0.61, A-B r=0.37) and the consistent ordering in the downstream UER/PER tables support the claim that D(E)/vec(E) are better suited to EMG-to-speech mapping than spectrogram features.
The ethical statement is reasonably thorough, and the paper is written in a way that makes the pipeline (TDS + CTC + pretrained HuBERT units + vocoder) easy to follow and reproduce in principle.
weaknesses: The central claim of the paper — end-to-end EMG-to-speech synthesis — is never actually evaluated. No intelligibility or perceptual quality metrics (WER, CER, MOS, listening tests, or even example audios) are reported. UER of ~59% and PER of ~41% are extremely high, so it is not established that the decoded dis(H) units produce intelligible speech. The 'Continuing work' section concedes this, which means the paper's headline claim is currently unsupported by evidence.

Reproducibility is undermined: the dataset and code are only promised 'upon completion of the project' (footnote 2) and are not available at review time, contradicting the paper's own criticism of prior work for using private datasets and lacking reproducible benchmarks. No baseline comparisons against prior EMG-to-speech systems are provided either.

Key experimental details are missing or ambiguous: the number of subjects contributing to the main section-3 dataset is never stated; it is unclear whether reported UER/PER (and their ± values) are averaged over subjects or runs, and whether results are single-subject or speaker-independent — a critical distinction for this field.

The interpretation that SS representations 'implicitly encode articulatory mechanisms' is overstated relative to the evidence. A strong envelope/power correlation between H and D(E) could arise from global acoustic-energy coupling rather than articulatory encoding; no control analyses (e.g., conditioning on energy, using non-speech signals, or shuffled baselines) are provided. Moreover, prior work the authors cite [24, 25] already established articulatory content in SS models, limiting the novelty of the core finding.

The linear-probing design has a mismatch the authors themselves acknowledge in footnote 4: the intended target vec(E) is intractable, so D(E) is substituted as a 'proxy' — the justification is plausible but the probe is not actually testing the claimed relationship directly.

Figure 2 shows t-SNE for a single subject only; clustering accuracy (70.6–73.7%) is reported as an average across 12 subjects but with no per-subject variance, and k-medoids 'classification accuracy' on 13 gestures without subject normalization may partly reflect subject-specific covariate structure rather than gesture separability.

Several presentation defects suggest the manuscript is not ready: broken sentence in the ethical statement ('Institutional Review Board Administration protocol .'), an empty Conflict of Interest section, an incorrect vocoder citation (Tacotron [10] is an acoustic model, not a vocoder; the actual unit-to-waveform model is unspecified), and inconsistent electrode counts (31 vs. 22 channels across experiments) that require careful footnote reading to reconcile.
Scope of claims vs. evidence: the introduction promises applications to laryngectomy, dysarthria, and dysphonia populations, but all data come from healthy volunteers with no clinical validation.

strengths: The open-sourced datasets are a major community contribution: a ~9-hour, ~6,800-word EMG-to-speech corpus from a healthy participant plus ~1 hour from an ALS participant, released with code, data, synthesized audio, and human transcriptions — addressing a widely acknowledged reproducibility gap in EMG/silent-speech research.

The paper targets a genuinely harder and clinically motivated setting: alignment-free EMG-to-speech synthesis without paired, time-synchronized EMG-audio supervision, which prior EMG benchmarks (Gaddy and Klein) do not address.

The probing analysis is a novel and interesting finding: a strong linear relationship (r = 0.85) between S3 representations and EMG power, with layer-wise structure that plausibly connects to why HuBERT layer 6 is optimal for resynthesis in prior work. This adds interpretive evidence about what S3 models encode.
Phoneme-guided decoding is a simple, well-motivated, articulatorily grounded technique with a statistically significant improvement (UER 56.08 -> 51.81) on both corpora.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough and multi-faceted: UER/PER with 5 seeds, human transcription WER/PER with three raters, MOS with 10 raters, ablations on training-data size, loss curves, and an EMG2TEXT comparison using a WFST decoder.

The paper is unusually transparent about limitations (single participants, no longitudinal analysis, no comparison of WER across studies) and about the non-comparability of contextual WERs with invasive BCI work.
Rigorous ethical treatment: IRB protocol, informed consent for publication of deidentified data, and detailed participant criteria.
weaknesses: Absolute system performance remains weak: 51-62% WER and ~50% UER mean roughly every other word is misrecognized. The clinical-utility claim is therefore aspirational; the contribution rests more on the dataset, analysis, and methodology than on a usable system.

All headline results come from a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant; no cross-participant generalization, electrode-shift robustness test, or day-to-day non-stationarity analysis is provided, which is a substantial threat to the claimed practical significance.

The training targets are derived from gTTS audio of the transcripts rather than subject-recorded audio, and are temporally unaligned with the EMG. While motivated by clinical scenarios, this weakens the interpretation of speech-quality results and makes WER partly dependent on HuBERT-unit behavior on synthetic speech; the paper does not quantify this confound.

Some interpretive claims are stronger than the evidence: the 'principled interpretation' of the layer-6 peak rests on a correlation from one participant, and the argument that phoneme-guided decoding helps 'because EMG captures phonetic structure more faithfully than HuBERT units' is asserted rather than tested against alternatives.

The contextual comparisons to invasive interfaces (Wairagkar et al., Metzger et al.) are fair-minded but could still invite misreading; they differ in vocabulary constraints, evaluation protocol, and data scale, and are not apples-to-apples.

The shift-tolerant module is applied to covariance features (vec(E)) whose entries are channel-indexed; circularly shifting a flattened covariance matrix does not correspond to a meaningful electrode displacement for off-diagonal terms, and this design choice is not analyzed.

MOS evaluation covers only 35 of 460 sentences, and the MOS-vs-WER dissociation is explained narratively rather than experimentally; a direct intelligibility-quality comparison against a vocoder-only or random-unit baseline would strengthen the interpretation.

strengths: The paper makes a genuinely valuable resource contribution: one of the largest openly available EMG-to-speech corpora (~9 hours / 6,800 unique words from a healthy speaker, ~1 hour from an ALS participant, plus a 12-participant orofacial gesture dataset), with project page, code, and data links, which substantially improves reproducibility in a field dominated by private datasets (Metzger et al., Littlejohn et al.).

The alignment-free problem setting is clinically well motivated (laryngectomy, silent articulation, degraded audio in ALS), and the paper is honest that this makes the learning problem harder and that its results are not directly comparable to prior work.

The linear probing analysis (H -> D(E), r = 0.85, layer-wise across HuBERT/wav2vec2/WavLM) is a clean, replicated-across-models analysis, and the connection between layer 6 articulatory structure and previously observed resynthesis optima (Lakhotia et al.) is a plausible, testable mechanistic hypothesis.

The methods are simple and use off-the-shelf components (HuBERT units, CTC, Tacotron vocoder, TDS convolutions), with reasonable architectural detail in Appendix D, multi-seed reporting (5 seeds), statistical significance for the phoneme-guided decoding improvement, and ablations on training-set size and losses.
Evaluation is multi-faceted (UER, PER, human WER, PER of transcriptions, MOS) and the paper transparently reports weak absolute numbers (e.g., 62.55% human WER) rather than cherry-picking.
Thorough limitations and ethics sections, including IRB, consent, and participant details.
weaknesses: Absolute system performance is weak: ~62% human-rated WER on the healthy large-vocabulary corpus and ~52% on the small-vocabulary ALS corpus (with only 300 unique words) means the synthesized speech is far from practically intelligible. The system is best viewed as a baseline, yet the framing (neuromuscular speech interface restoring communication) oversells current utility.

The central 'insight' is only loosely coupled to the best-performing method: the strongest decoding uses vec(E) (961-dim), not D(E), and the pipeline (EMG -> HuBERT units -> vocoder) largely replicates the Metzger et al. (2023) recipe. The articulatorily 'grounded' D(E) representation performs on par or worse, so the causal link between the probing analysis and encoder design is more narrative than demonstrated.

The novelty of the probing claim ('for the first time, a quantitative relationship between EMG and S3 representations') is incremental relative to Cho et al. (2023, 2024), which already established that S3 models encode articulation (via EMA); extending this to EMG is useful but a modest step.

No controlled comparison on their own data against a time-aligned supervised baseline (e.g., a Gaddy & Klein-style model), so the cost/benefit of the alignment-free setting and the relative advantage of the proposed design choices cannot be quantified; comparisons to prior work are qualitative and explicitly not one-to-one.

Evaluation setup concerns: targets are gTTS audio rather than the participant's own voice, and the ALS WER advantage over the healthy speaker is not analyzed; it likely reflects the much smaller/controlled vocabulary rather than better decoding, and raters transcribing could partially exploit topical/syntactic predictability. Raters were also the only listeners for WER while MOS used different raters on a small 35-sentence subset.

Some claims exceed the evidence: the 'principled interpretation' of the layer-6 peak is correlational; the generalization of conclusions rests on a single healthy participant and a single ALS participant; and validation losses rise after ~25 epochs while models train for 50, leaving checkpoint-selection details ambiguous.

For an ACL audience, the work is closer to a neuroengineering/benchmark paper; the linguistic/NLP contribution (phoneme-guided decoding, +4.3 UER) is real but modest and heuristic (fixed loss weights 0.8/0.1/0.1 without tuning analysis).

strengths: The paper releases one of the largest publicly available EMG-to-speech corpora (9 hours / ~6,800-word vocabulary from a healthy participant, plus an ALS corpus with silent articulation), addressing a genuine resource gap in a field dominated by private, non-reproducible datasets.

The analysis relating EMG covariance features to self-supervised speech representations is a nice empirical contribution: the linear probing (r = 0.85 between S3 representations and EMG power) and the k-medoids clustering of orofacial gestures (73.7% vs. 7.69% chance) provide interpretable evidence that S3 models encode articulatory structure.

Phoneme-guided decoding is a reasonable, well-motivated technique grounded in articulatory structure, and the reported improvement (56.08% to 51.81% UER, p < 10^-6) is statistically supported with 5 seeds.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: human transcription-based WER across three raters, PER analysis, MOS ratings, an alignment-free training setting motivated by clinical scenarios, an emg2text WFST-decoding comparison, and training-data-size ablations.
Demonstration on a participant with ALS silently articulating speech is clinically meaningful and strengthens the broader impact case; ethical considerations and limitations are candidly discussed.
Appendix D provides substantial implementation detail (architecture, optimization, loss weights, preprocessing), supporting reproducibility alongside the released code and data.
weaknesses: The headline synthesis results are weak in absolute terms: ~52-56% UER and ~62% human-rated WER on the general corpus means the system is far from intelligible open-vocabulary speech, and the paper's own emg2text baseline (WER 51.17%) outperforms the direct synthesis pipeline, so the practical value of end-to-end synthesis over the text pathway is not demonstrated.

Training targets are derived from gTTS synthetic audio rather than subject-recorded audio, which weakens claims about 'synthesizing speech' - the vocoder and unit targets are learned from low-quality synthetic speech, and naturalness/intelligibility ceiling is unclear; the paper does not quantify how much this hurts.

Key scientific claims are partially overreached: the probing uses D(E) as a proxy for vec(E) for dimensionality reasons (acknowledged in a footnote), and the interpretation that HuBERT layer 6's success is 'explained' by articulatory encoding is speculative; correlation with EMG power may partly reflect loudness/voicing confounds rather than articulator-specific structure.

The main corpus comes from a single healthy participant and the ALS corpus from a single participant, with small test sets (400 and 60 sentences); generalization across speakers, sessions, and electrode placements is untested and acknowledged only in limitations.

Comparisons to prior work are explicitly not one-to-one, and no baseline (e.g., spectrogram-pipeline or ablation of the shift-tolerant module) is evaluated in the same alignment-free setting beyond feature-input ablations; the 5.3 comparisons are thus contextual rather than evidence of superiority.

MOS is computed on only 35 sentences with raters who had prior exposure constraints, and the explanation for moderate MOS despite high WER is post-hoc; the interpretability of MOS in this setting remains murky.

Some framing oversells novelty: the alignment-free pipeline closely follows Metzger et al. (2023)/Littlejohn et al. (2025) with HuBERT discrete units and a pretrained vocoder, and the probing findings echo Cho et al. (2023, 2024); the core methodological delta is the EMG covariance representation and phoneme-guided decoding.
